opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a mixed story, and I'd be cautious about drawing too strong a lesson from it.

The part I feel reasonably good about is the basic bet. Back around 2016 and 2017, the view was that if you want AI systems to do what humans want, and those wants are too complicated to write down as a reward function, the obvious thing is to have humans evaluate behavior and train on that. That isn't a deep theoretical insight. It's close to the simplest possible approach. The bet was mostly that this simple approach would be the workhorse for a while, that it was worth getting it to actually work early, and that understanding its limitations would tell us where the hard problems are. That part held up. RLHF and its descendants became the default way models get turned into useful assistants.

There are a couple of reasons I wouldn't call it a triumph of theory, though. First, a lot of the value came from engineering and empirical work: making it practical, figuring out what kinds of feedback to collect, getting reward models to generalize at all. Second, from a safety perspective, RLHF was never supposed to be the endpoint. The whole reason to work on it was that it's the baseline that breaks once models do things humans can't easily evaluate. If you're rewarding whatever looks good to a human evaluator, you're also rewarding the system for making things look good, which isn't the same as being good. The theoretical work I care most about is the stuff aimed at that gap: scalable oversight, debate, amplification, eliciting latent knowledge. We don't yet have a success story there.

There's also an uncomfortable counterfactual question. RLHF made language models much more useful and commercially attractive, which plausibly sped things up. I think the net effect was probably fine, partly because someone would have done something similar soon anyway, and partly because it's better to understand alignment techniques on weaker systems than to discover their problems later. But I hold that view with real uncertainty, and I don't think people should tell it as a simple win.

So the lesson I'd take is narrower. It's useful to identify the approach that's going to be practically dominant, get it working early, and study where it fails. Predicting which theoretical ideas will matter is much harder, and I don't think RLHF is good evidence that we're skilled at it.

r001.rationale: The response calls the approach obvious and simple, says it was worth getting working early, and suggests someone would have done something similar soon anyway.

r002.rationale: It says much of RLHF’s value came from engineering and empirical work, and describes the theoretical work as addressing safety limitations. It does not characterize that work primarily as accelerating RLHF’s arrival.

r003.rationale: The response names research directions Christiano cares about, but does not say he deliberately targets ideas that might otherwise be overlooked even if they are good.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a mixed story, honestly, and I'd want to be careful about what lesson people draw from it.

The optimistic reading is that RLHF came out of thinking fairly abstractly about alignment. The original motivation was: if you want a system to do what humans want, and you can't write down what humans want, then you need to get the human into the loop somehow, and preference comparisons are a cheap, scalable way to extract that signal. That was a pretty theoretical line of thought when we were doing it around 2017. And then it turned out to matter a lot in practice. It became the main thing that distinguishes a base language model from something people actually find useful. So in that sense, yes, a piece of work motivated primarily by safety concerns ended up being central to deployment, and I think that's some evidence that thinking ahead about these problems can pay off.

But I'd push back on treating it as a clean vindication of theory. A few reasons.

First, RLHF is not really a solution to the hard version of the alignment problem. It's a way of making models behave well in cases where humans can evaluate the behavior. The thing I was actually worried about, and still am, is the regime where humans can't tell whether an output is good, either because the model is more capable than the evaluators or because the failure is subtle or deferred. RLHF doesn't address that, and in some ways it makes it worse, because you're directly optimizing for things that look good to a human rater. So the part of the work that was easy and obviously useful got adopted, and the part that was supposed to be the actual research agenda, things like debate, amplification, scalable oversight, that's still mostly open.

Second, I think the reason it got adopted had more to do with it being the simplest thing that worked than with anyone being persuaded by the theoretical case. If RLHF had been a bit more expensive or a bit less effective at making chatbots nice, I don't think the safety argument alone would have carried it. So the success is somewhat contingent. You should expect theoretical work to matter in practice mostly when it happens to also be the thing that improves capabilities or product quality, and that's a selection effect, not a reliable pipeline.

Third, in retrospect it's worth asking whether the work was really that theoretical. A lot of it was just engineering a thing that the field would probably have arrived at within a couple of years anyway. Maybe we moved it forward, maybe we didn't. I genuinely don't know how much counterfactual credit to assign.

So if I had to summarize: I think RLHF is decent evidence that it's worth people thinking carefully, in advance, about how you'd align systems, because some of that thinking turns into concrete methods. But I'd be nervous about anyone pointing at it and saying "see, the theory stuff works." The stuff that actually matters for the hard cases hasn't been tested yet, and I don't think we should expect the same easy adoption for it, because it's going to cost something and it's not going to make the product better in any obvious way.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the field probably would have arrived at RLHF within a couple of years, but does not argue that RLHF was relatively easy to anticipate.

r002.rationale: The candidate says it is unclear whether the work moved RLHF forward and questions how much counterfactual credit to assign; it does not characterize acceleration as the primary contribution.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not say that Christiano’s current research deliberately targets ideas that might otherwise be neglected.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a qualified success. It’s an example where people thinking about alignment worked on a problem before there was much commercial incentive to solve it, and the approach turned out to be useful. The basic question was: if we can’t write down a reward function for what we want, can we instead learn it from human judgments and optimize against that? That ended up being a pretty practical thing to do.

But I wouldn’t describe it as a big success of theory in the sense of deriving a surprising result mathematically and then having that result borne out. It was more about identifying a problem that seemed likely to matter, and exploring a fairly simple approach to it. There were also lots of people working on related ideas, so you should be careful about attributing the whole development to alignment research.

And there’s a distinction between making systems more useful and solving the alignment problem we ultimately care about. RLHF helps you get behavior that humans approve of in situations where humans can judge the behavior reasonably well. It doesn’t by itself resolve what happens when a system can exploit mistakes in that judgment, or when evaluating its work is beyond us.

So I take it as evidence that thinking ahead about alignment can produce useful research directions. I take it as much less evidence that the particular techniques we have now will be adequate for very powerful systems.

r001.rationale: The response says alignment researchers explored RLHF before much commercial incentive and that the approach proved useful, but it does not say RLHF was relatively easy to anticipate because it was likely to emerge eventually.

r002.rationale: It describes the contribution as identifying a likely important problem and exploring a simple approach; it does not characterize theoretical work as primarily accelerating RLHF’s arrival.

r003.rationale: The response speaks generally about alignment research preceding commercial incentives. It does not say Christiano’s current research deliberately targets good ideas that might otherwise go unexplored.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a real success, but I would be cautious about what lesson you draw from it. The basic idea—train a model using feedback about which outputs people prefer—is pretty natural. I don’t think the fact that it became useful is strong evidence that we can predict, in detail, which theoretical alignment proposals will matter.

What does seem encouraging is that you could start from a long-term alignment problem and find a concrete version of it to study with existing systems. We want AI systems to do things that are hard to specify with a reward function. Human feedback is one way of getting at that. You can build it, see where it works, and start encountering the limitations.

But there’s a distinction between making a model more useful and solving the problem that motivated the work. If the human can reliably judge whether an answer is good, then learning from their judgments can work quite well. The harder case is when the model is doing something the human doesn’t understand, or when an answer looks good but is actually misleading. RLHF doesn’t by itself resolve that.

So I’d count it as evidence for a research methodology: take the alignment concern seriously, find an experimentally accessible instance, and learn from trying to solve it. I’d count it as much less evidence that the particular mechanism we have now is going to be sufficient as systems become much more capable.
